title: Food Chains, Energy Flow & Biological Magnification

ask.question: What common garden animal might eat the grasshopper, and what eats that animal next?
ask.expect: A frog or bird eats the grasshopper, and a snake eats the frog.
ask.hint: Think of a small amphibian or reptile that snaps up garden insects.

options.text: A frog eats the grasshopper, and a snake eats the frog.
options.why: That forms a clear line of who eats whom in nature.

options.text: The grasshopper turns into soil and feeds the plants directly.
options.why: Grasshoppers get eaten by primary carnivores like frogs before decomposers break down what remains.

title: Food Chains, Energy Flow & Biological Magnification

ask.question: If plants have 10,000 J of energy, how much reaches the herbivores?
ask.expect: 1,000 Joules.
ask.hint: Calculate 10 percent of 10,000.

options.text: 1,000 Joules
options.why: Ten percent of 10,000 J is exactly 1,000 J.

options.text: 100 Joules
options.why: 100 Joules would be only 1 percent of 10,000 J, but 10 percent is passed.

options.text: 9,000 Joules
options.why: 9,000 Joules is the amount lost to metabolic processes, leaving 10 percent for the consumer.

title: Food Chains, Energy Flow & Biological Magnification

ask.question: Why are food chains usually limited to 3 or 4 steps?
ask.expect: Because so little usable energy remains after 3 or 4 levels that it cannot support another population.
ask.hint: Look at the remaining energy at the top — would a fifth animal get enough food to survive?

options.text: The energy remaining after 3 to 4 levels is too small to sustain another trophic level.
options.why: Because 90% is lost at every step, very little usable energy remains at the top.

options.text: There are no predators strong enough to hunt the top animals.
options.why: The limit is thermodynamic and energetic, not about physical strength.

title: Food Chains, Energy Flow & Biological Magnification

ask.question: How does an interconnected food web help a predator survive when one prey species drops?
ask.expect: The predator can switch to feeding on other available prey in the web, like mice or insects.
ask.hint: Check the other arrows pointing into the hawk.

options.text: The hawk can feed on alternative prey like mice or small birds in the web.
options.why: Alternative pathways provide ecosystem stability.

options.text: The hawk begins eating plants directly instead.
options.why: Carnivores cannot switch their digestive biology to become primary producers.

title: Food Chains, Energy Flow & Biological Magnification

ask.question: Which organism in a food chain accumulates the maximum concentration of non-biodegradable pesticides?
ask.expect: The organism at the top trophic level (top consumer / humans).
ask.hint: Think about where the chemicals pile up after passing through every lower level.

options.text: The top consumer or humans at the highest trophic level.
options.why: Because toxins cannot be broken down and accumulate progressively at each higher level.

options.text: The primary producers because they absorb it first.
options.why: Producers have the lowest concentration per organism; it concentrates as higher consumers eat many of them.

ask.question: What two substances react together when magnesium burns in air, and what new substance is formed?
ask.expect: Magnesium reacts with oxygen in the air to produce magnesium oxide.
ask.hint: Think about what gas in the air is needed for any burning reaction.

options.text: Magnesium and oxygen react to make magnesium oxide.
options.why: That's it: magnesium combines with atmospheric oxygen to yield magnesium oxide.

options.text: Magnesium and carbon dioxide make magnesium oxide.
options.why: Burning in air relies on oxygen gas, not carbon dioxide.
options.hint: Which gas in air supports combustion?

options.text: Magnesium alone turns into ash without reacting.
options.why: Burning is a combination with oxygen gas from the surrounding air.
options.hint: Where does the extra mass and oxygen in magnesium oxide come from?

ask.question: When zinc granules react with dilute sulphuric acid to produce zinc sulphate and hydrogen gas, what are the chemical formulae of the two reactants on the LHS?
ask.expect: Zn and H2SO4
ask.hint: What is the symbol for zinc, and what is the formula for sulphuric acid?

options.text: Zn and H2SO4
options.why: Zinc is Zn and sulphuric acid is H2SO4; together they form the reactants on the left.

options.text: Zn and HCl
options.why: HCl is hydrochloric acid, but the reaction specifies sulphuric acid, which is H2SO4.
options.hint: Remember sulphate contains SO4.

options.text: ZnSO4 and H2
options.why: ZnSO4 and H2 are the products formed on the right side, not the starting reactants.
options.hint: Which substances are we starting with before the reaction occurs?

ask.question: If solid iron reacts with steam (gaseous water) to form solid iron oxide and hydrogen gas, what state symbol belongs right after steam: (l) or (g)?
ask.expect: (g) because steam is water in its gaseous state.
ask.hint: Think about what steam physically is compared to liquid water in a glass.

options.text: (g) because steam is gaseous water
options.why: Steam is water in the gas phase, so it gets the symbol (g).

options.text: (l) because water is naturally a liquid
options.why: Even though water is liquid at room temperature, steam in this reaction is a gas, so it must be marked (g).
options.hint: What state is steam in during this high-temperature reaction?

options.text: (aq) because water is a solvent
options.why: Aqueous denotes something dissolved in water, not water itself.
options.hint: Is steam a solution or pure water vapor?

ask.question: In the reaction CO(g) + 2H2(g) -> CH3OH(l), where should the condition '340 atm' be written in the equation?
ask.expect: Above or below the reaction arrow.
ask.hint: Where do special conditions like temperature and pressure sit in a chemical equation?

options.text: Above or below the arrow connecting reactants and products.
options.why: Reaction conditions like pressure (340 atm) are always indicated directly above or below the arrow.

options.text: Next to the reactants on the left side with a plus sign.
options.why: Pressure is an operating condition, not a chemical reactant, so it cannot be added with a plus sign.
options.hint: Does pressure have a chemical formula like a reactant?

options.text: In brackets after the product CH3OH.
options.why: Brackets after chemical formulas are reserved for state symbols like (l) or (g).
options.hint: Brackets after compounds indicate physical states, not external conditions.

ask.question: Did that missing mass actually vanish from the universe, or where did it go?
ask.expect: The missing mass escaped into the air as smoke, carbon dioxide, and water vapor.
ask.hint: Think about what rises up from a fire as the wood burns.

options.text: The mass turned into smoke and gases that escaped into the air
options.why: The atoms in the wood combined with oxygen to form gases like carbon dioxide and steam that floated away.

options.text: The mass was destroyed by the heat of the fire
options.why: Heat cannot destroy atoms; chemical reactions only rearrange atoms into new substances like gases.

options.text: The log converted directly into pure heat and light energy
options.why: In ordinary chemical reactions, atoms are never converted into energy; they just escape as unseen gases.

ask.question: Why is the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O incomplete as it stands?
ask.expect: One oxygen atom on the reactant side is unaccounted for on the product side.
ask.hint: Compare the number of oxygen atoms on the left with the number on the right.

options.text: Because there are two oxygen atoms on the left but only one on the right
options.why: An oxygen atom cannot vanish; our equation must account for both oxygen atoms.

options.text: Because hydrogen and oxygen cannot react directly
options.why: Hydrogen and oxygen react readily to form water; the issue is simply that our atom tally does not match.

options.text: Because water is H2O2 instead of H2O
options.why: Water is strictly H2O; H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, an entirely different substance.

ask.question: What number coefficient must we put in front of H2 on the left to get 4 hydrogen atoms?
ask.expect: A coefficient of 2 in front of H2.
ask.hint: Each H2 molecule brings 2 hydrogen atoms. How many molecules make 4 atoms?

options.text: Put a 2 in front of H2
options.why: 2 times H2 gives exactly 4 hydrogen atoms, matching the right side perfectly.

options.text: Change H2 to H4
options.why: We cannot alter subscripts because H4 is not a stable molecular formula for hydrogen gas.

options.text: Put a 4 in front of H2
options.why: 4 H2 would give 8 hydrogen atoms, which is too many.

ask.question: What coefficient should we place in front of O2 on the left side to get 4 oxygen atoms?
ask.expect: A coefficient of 2 in front of O2.
ask.hint: Each O2 molecule contains 2 oxygen atoms. What times 2 equals 4?

options.text: Put a 2 in front of O2
options.why: 2 times 2 gives 4 oxygen atoms, completing the balance for all elements.

options.text: Put a 4 in front of O2
options.why: 4 O2 would give 8 oxygen atoms on the left, but we only have 4 on the right.

options.text: Put a 1 in front of O2
options.why: 1 O2 gives only 2 oxygen atoms, which leaves the equation short by 2 oxygens.

ask.question: When charcoal burns completely in oxygen, what single gas is formed?
ask.expect: Carbon dioxide gas is formed when carbon reacts with oxygen.
ask.hint: What gas do you exhale and what gas forms when carbon joins with oxygen?

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas
options.why: Carbon combines directly with oxygen gas from the air to form one single product: carbon dioxide.

options.text: Carbon monoxide only
options.why: Carbon monoxide forms only in limited oxygen, but complete burning in air produces carbon dioxide.
options.hint: Think about the common gas formed when carbon fully burns in abundant air.

options.text: Ash and smoke only, no gas
options.why: Ash is just the mineral residue left behind; the main carbon turns into carbon dioxide gas.
options.hint: The carbon itself combines with oxygen in the air to escape as an invisible gas.

ask.question: What is the key feature on the product side of every combination reaction?
ask.expect: There is only one single product formed.
ask.hint: Count how many distinct compounds or elements are produced on the right-hand side of the arrow.

options.text: Only one single product is formed
options.why: No matter how many reactants combine on the left, a combination reaction always yields exactly one single product on the right.

options.text: Two products are always formed
options.why: If two products form, substances have exchanged parts or decomposed, not simply combined into one.
options.hint: Look at the general form A + B -> AB again.

options.text: There are always two reactants and two products
options.why: The reactants can be two or more, but the defining rule is that they unite into a single product.
options.hint: Focus on the right side of the chemical arrow.

ask.question: What does the sharp rise in temperature tell us about this combination reaction?
ask.expect: It shows that the reaction is exothermic, meaning it releases heat energy.
ask.hint: Think about what kind of reaction releases heat into its surroundings.

options.text: It is an exothermic reaction that releases heat
options.why: Reactions in which heat is released along with the formation of products are called exothermic reactions.

options.text: It is an endothermic reaction absorbing heat
options.why: An endothermic reaction absorbs heat and makes the container colder, whereas here heat is released.
options.hint: Does heat entering or leaving the mixture make the container feel hot?

options.text: It means the water is boiling on its own
options.why: The heat comes from the chemical bond formation between calcium oxide and water, not from external heating.
options.hint: The chemical reaction itself produces this heat.

ask.question: Which reaction is a combination reaction: Reaction 1, 2, or 3?
ask.expect: Reaction 2 (burning of magnesium) because magnesium and oxygen combine to form a single product, magnesium oxide.
ask.hint: Look for the reaction that has two reactants on the left but only one single product on the right.

options.text: Reaction 2 (2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO) because it forms only one single product
options.why: Two substances, magnesium and oxygen, combine to yield only one product: magnesium oxide (MgO).

options.text: Reaction 1 because it has oxygen in it
options.why: Reaction 1 produces both CO2 and H2O, so two products are formed, making it a combustion reaction, not combination.
options.hint: Check how many different products appear on the right side.

options.text: Reaction 3 because zinc combines with sulfate
options.why: Reaction 3 is a displacement reaction where zinc displaces copper, producing two separate substances.
options.hint: Remember the golden rule: combination reactions must produce only ONE single product.

ask.question: If a stronger player claims a chair from someone already seated, what happens to the person who was sitting there?
ask.expect: The person who was already sitting there gets pushed out or displaced.
ask.hint: Does the person stay on the chair, or do they have to get up and leave?

options.text: They are pushed off their seat and have to step aside.
options.why: Exactly, they lose their spot because someone stronger took their place.

options.text: Both of them share the chair peacefully.
options.why: In musical chairs, only one person gets to keep the seat — the stronger or faster one pushes the other out.
options.hint: Can two people keep the same spot in musical chairs?

ask.question: What is the reddish-brown substance that coats the iron nail?
ask.expect: It is metallic copper displaced from the copper sulphate solution.
ask.hint: Which metal was combined in the blue solution before iron went in?

options.text: It is copper metal settling on the nail.
options.why: Yes! Copper was in the liquid, and now it has been pushed out as solid metal onto the nail.

options.text: It is rust formed from iron reacting with water.
options.why: Rust is an oxide of iron, but here copper metal itself is displaced from the solution and deposits on the nail.
options.hint: What metal was present inside the blue copper sulphate solution?

ask.question: If you put copper into iron sulphate solution, will a displacement reaction occur? Why or why not?
ask.expect: No reaction occurs because copper is less reactive than iron.
ask.hint: Can a weaker metal kick out a more reactive metal from its compound?

options.text: No reaction will occur because copper is less reactive than iron.
options.why: Spot on. A less reactive metal cannot displace a more reactive metal from its salt solution.

options.text: Yes, it will turn blue and form copper sulphate.
options.why: Copper cannot displace iron because iron holds on more strongly due to being more reactive.
options.hint: Remember, only the more reactive metal has the power to displace.

ask.question: What products are formed when lead reacts with copper chloride (Pb + CuCl2)?
ask.expect: Lead chloride (PbCl2) and copper metal (Cu).
ask.hint: Lead replaces copper, so lead combines with chlorine while copper is released.

options.text: Lead chloride and copper metal.
options.why: Exactly. Lead combines with chloride to form PbCl2, leaving copper as solid metal.

options.text: Lead copper and chlorine gas.
options.why: Metals don't combine into an alloy solution like that here — lead displaces copper to bind with chlorine as PbCl2.
options.hint: Which part did copper leave behind for lead to pair with?

ask.question: If you mix two clear, see-through liquids, what do you usually expect to see?
ask.expect: The mixture remains clear and transparent.
ask.hint: Does dissolving two clear things suddenly make a solid object appear, or does it stay liquid and see-through?

options.text: It stays a clear liquid
options.why: Exactly. Usually, mixing two clear solutions just gives another clear mixture.

options.text: It turns into a solid lump
options.why: Normally mixing two clear solutions doesn't create solids — unless a specific chemical reaction takes place.

ask.question: What is the general name for a reaction that produces an insoluble solid precipitate?
ask.expect: A precipitation reaction.
ask.hint: It is named directly after the word precipitate.

options.text: Precipitation reaction
options.why: Yes! Any chemical reaction that forms an insoluble solid is classified as a precipitation reaction.

options.text: Neutralisation reaction
options.why: Neutralisation is specifically acid plus base; when an insoluble solid forms, it is called a precipitation reaction.

ask.question: In your own words, what happens between the reactants in a double displacement reaction?
ask.expect: There is a mutual exchange of ions between the two reactants.
ask.hint: Think about what the positive and negative ions do with their partners.

options.text: The reactants exchange their ions with each other
options.why: Exactly. The positive and negative ions swap partners between the two compounds.

options.text: One more reactive metal pushes out a less reactive one
options.why: That is single displacement. In double displacement, both compounds mutually swap their ions.

ask.question: Why is BaSO4 written as solid (s) in the equation, while NaCl is written as aqueous (aq)?
ask.expect: Barium sulphate is insoluble and forms a solid precipitate, while sodium chloride remains dissolved in water.
ask.hint: Which one formed the white solid that settled at the bottom?

options.text: BaSO4 is the insoluble white precipitate, and NaCl stays dissolved in water
options.why: Precisely. BaSO4 does not dissolve in water, so it falls out as a solid precipitate, while NaCl stays dissolved.

options.text: BaSO4 is a gas and NaCl is a liquid
options.why: Neither is a gas. BaSO4 is an insoluble solid precipitate, and NaCl is a salt dissolved in water.
